ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox will start Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez in the series against the Guardians that starts Tuesday at Fenway Park.
That would conceivably line them up for the Wild Card Series that starts on Sept. 29 with six days rest each.
“Don’t read into that yet,” interim manager Chad Tracy said Sunday before a 5-1 loss against the Rays. “We can line that up still however we want.”
True. But Tolle has a 2.44 ERA in his last eight starts. He also has faced the Yankees twice this season and allowed one run on four hits over 13 innings with three walks and 18 strikeouts.
Gray allowed three runs on nine hits over 13⅔ innings in two starts against the Yankees. He struck out 12 and walked three.
Guerrero returns
Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero returned from a 19-day stint on the injured list with shoulder inflammation. Righthanded reliever Wyatt Olds was optioned to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero pitched a perfect eighth inning, striking out two.
“Felt good to be out there,” Guerrero said. “If I get a few more games I’ll be fine [for the postseason].”
Guerrero, 35, was called up in May for his first major league stint since 2019. He emerged as a reliable late-inning option, posting a 3.18 ERA over 39 games.
“He’s obviously a very important piece to this puzzle in our bullpen,” Tracy said.
Olds deserved a better fate. The 27-year-old has a 1.20 ERA and 1.20 WHIP in 13 games since making his major league debut on Aug. 17.
“Very tough. He’s thrown the ball great. He’s got big stuff,” Tracy said. “We had to make a roster decision.”
Contreras doing better
Willson Contreras took some swings in the batting cage to test his bruised right hand and came through fine. He said he hopes to be able to do more on Tuesday. “Step in the right direction,” Tracy said … There was no update on Garrett Crochet, who has yet to face hitters. That could come in the next few days … Tanner Houck had a 3.38 ERA over eight innings in four minor league games. Tracy suggested he would face hitters in a simulated game early this week. “Figuring out the next steps at home — and want to figure that out — but no plans for the next outing,” Tracy said. Could Houck be activated? “It’s possible,” Tracy said. “At this point, it’s going to depend very much on where’s the roster at, what are the needs, and then go from there.”… Rays shortstop Taylor Walls showed his baseball acumen in the first inning. With Roman Anthony on first and one out, he allowed Adley Rutschman’s popup to drop. Walls picked up the ball and flipped to second to get the force on Anthony. That left the Sox with a slower runner on first. It ultimately didn’t matter as Trevor Story struck out … Worcester, as Double-A Portland also did last weekend, had its final game rained out. The WooSox finished 76-67. Kutter Crawford was at Polar Park, and the plan was to have him start what would have been a bullpen game. Crawford has not appeared in a major league game since Sept. 28, 2024. He missed the 2025 season because of an injured right knee. He injured his right wrist in August of that season doing yard work at his home in Florida. Crawford pitched three innings in a rehab game for Worcester on April 11 but had a setback and wasn’t cleared for a game until Sunday. “He got to a point where he wanted to go out there and throw one,” Tracy said.

The Boston Red Sox will face off against the Tampa Bay Rays on Sunday in a rubber match on the road and the Red Sox got a reinforcement back just in time for the series finale.
Boston has been missing 2026 breakout flamethrower Tyron Guerrero since Aug. 31. That will change on Sunday afternoon. The Red Sox announced that Guerrero is back and righty Wyatt Olds has been sent down to Triple-A in response.
"The Red Sox today reinstated RHP Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned RHP Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester," the Red Sox announced.
The Red Sox Got A Key Back
Over the last few weeks, much has been said about the reinforcements coming. Guerrero's return is the first example of this. The 6'8'' righty has a 3.26 ERA and a 36-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 38 2/3 innings pitched. It had been seven years since Guerrero had pitched in a big league game before the 2026 season. He last pitched in the majors back in 2019 with the Miami Marlins. He's been a breakout story for the Red Sox and now he's back.
Olds has been very good when he has been active on the big league roster this season. He has a 1.20 ERA in 13 appearances this season as a rookie, to go along with a 20-to-7 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 15 innings pitched.
Guerrero is the first reinforcement back for the bullpen, but he isn't likely to be the last. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are two other guys who could be back in the not-so-distant future. Houck is closer than Crochet is. Houck has been on a minor league rehab assignment. Crochet has been tossing bullpens, but hasn't advanced to facing live hitters just yet.
Olds has been good, but it was known that difficult bullpen decisions would be coming. This is the first and we should see more in the coming days.
Guerrero went from unknown among the Red Sox's fanbase, to a high-leverage guy for Boston fairly quickly. Now, he's back as Boston has a chance to clinch a spot in the postseason on Sunday afternoon against the Rays. If the Red Sox take down Tampa Bay, they will officially punch their ticket. Boston's magic number is down to one. A win will get them into the playoffs. Even if they lose, they can make it in on Sunday with losses by other clubs fighting for the Wild Card spots. It could be a big day for Boston and Guerrero's back.

The Red Sox’ magic number is one.
The Rays, armed with the best record in the American League, are 8-2 in their last 10 games, including a 2-1 win Saturday over Boston. Brayan Bello gave the Sox a solid effort, fanning 11 over eight innings of work.

Patrick Sandoval will start for the Red Sox Sunday. He has gone six innings just once in his last six starts. He has allowed four runs in his last two starts. He has faced Tampa Bay once this season, surrendering four earned runs in five innings on July 18.

Red Sox Reinstate RHP Tyron Guerrero from 15-Day IL
BOSTON, MA—The Boston Red Sox today reinstated right-handed pitcher Tyron Guerrero from the 15-Day Injured List. To make room, Boston optioned right-handed pitcher Wyatt Olds to Triple-A Worcester.
Guerrero, 35, was placed on the 15-Day Injured List on September 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The right-hander has recorded a 3.26 ERA (14 ER/38.2 IP) with 36 strikeouts in 38 games for Boston this season. He has also posted a 0.92 ERA (2 ER/19.2 IP) with 22 strikeouts in 15 relief outings for Triple-A Worcester this year. Originally signed as an international free agent by the San Diego Padres in May 2010, the Colombia native owns a 5.10 ERA (82 ER/144.2 IP) with 147 strikeouts in 151 career Major League games with the Padres (2016), Miami Marlins (2018-19), and Red Sox (2026).
Olds, 27, has posted a 1.20 ERA (2 ER/15.0 IP) with 20 strikeouts in 13 relief outings for Boston this season, his Major League debut. The right-hander has also posted a 5.33 ERA (30 ER/50.2 IP) with 74 strikeouts in 39 games this year for Worcester. Selected by the Red Sox in the seventh round of the 2021 First-Year Player Draft, the Oklahoma native owns a 5.88 ERA (254 ER/389.0 IP) with 489 strikeouts in 185 career minor league games (42 starts).

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — When Roman Anthony returned to the Boston Red Sox three weeks ago after nearly four months on the injury list with a torn right finger ligament, it initially looked as if he had barely missed any time.
Through his first five games after he was activated Aug. 30 in New York, Anthony recorded four games with multiple hits, going 10-for-22 with two homers, two doubles and a triple. His methodical rehab, missing 101 games, paid dividends with a bat that was ready to perform.
Advertisement
But then, as so often happens in baseball, he fell out of rhythm at the plate, collecting just seven hits, including just one extra-base hit, in his next 56 plate appearances.
That’s why he found himself in an early batting practice session Friday afternoon with hitting coach John Soteropulos, tinkering in the cage with a few mechanical adjustments.
The work clicked.
Oh baby, Roman! pic.twitter.com/aP7bBEgZX0
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 18, 2026
Three pitches into the game, Anthony clubbed a solo homer for a lead, and in the second inning, he smacked a bases-loaded single to drive in two more runs as the Red Sox beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-2, snapping the Rays’ six-game win streak. The win inched the Red Sox closer to clinching a playoff berth. A Red Sox win Saturday, coupled with a Texas Rangers loss, would punch Boston’s ticket to the playoffs.
“We came out and looked really good offensively in the first part of that game, and there was a lot of energy in the dugout,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “I think guys feel it. We’re not done yet, but I definitely think they sniff it, and we’re wanting to get there for sure.”
With eight games left in the regular season, getting Anthony’s bat hot again, particularly as Willson Contreras remains day to day with a deeply bruised right hand, will be imperative for the Red Sox lineup in the postseason.
“He will,” Tracy said confidently about Anthony’s bat regaining momentum. “I mean, you see what he can do. It’s the game of baseball, there’s ebbs and flows. He came off the rehab, and for like five games, he looked fantastic. Then he went through some stuff, and now he’s starting to look good again. When he’s going well, you see the impact he can make.”
Before Soteropulos was elevated to lead hitting coach this season after an overhaul of the coaching staff, he was the minor-league hitting coordinator and worked closely with Anthony. That relationship has helped.
Advertisement
“Me and John have been working on some things, really since I have been back,” Anthony said. “He’s amazing. He’s somebody who knows my swing so well. We have been together since I came into this org, all throughout the minor leagues. Having somebody here, somebody who knows my swing and when to talk and when to tinker. Nobody knows me better than John.
“It’s such a constant game of adjustments and looking over a span of my last few at-bats, it obviously was not where I wanted to be. I was hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side, so I was trying to get away from that. Hitting early on the field with John and with Trevor (Story) definitely helped.”
Anthony’s first-inning homer came off the bat at an estimated 107.7 mph with an estimated distance of 438 feet, marking the longest homer of his career.
But to him, the two-run single was just as important. In a rough series in Texas, the Red Sox had gone just 1-for-18 with runners in scoring position. His goal was to alleviate some pressure on the offense by simply making contact.
“That’s my job, to do everything I can to put the ball in play and find ways on base,” he said. “That’s how I have had a lot of success in the past as a leadoff hitter. So over these last games, just keep putting an emphasis on being the best leadoff hitter I can be. See as many pitches I can and try and get on base. It was a huge way to start the game. This game is all about momentum, so any time you can get something like that going, it’s huge.”
The two-run single gave the Red Sox the lead back after the Rays tied the score off Ranger Suarez in the bottom of the first. Jahmai Jones made it 4-1 in the third with his sixth homer of the year.
The insurance gave the Red Sox a cushion as Suarez was uncharacteristically spotty with command, walking a career-high five batters.
Advertisement
Still, he navigated traffic in each of the first four innings and allowed just the one run on three hits in 5 2/3 innings. Reliever Wyatt Olds wiggled out of a jam in the sixth after Suarez exited, walking two batters to load the bases, then falling behind pinch hitter Jake Fraley 3-1. Olds came back to strike out Fraley.
The Red Sox faced more trouble in the ninth, with reliever Erik Miller still searching for his command. Closer Aroldis Chapman remains day to day with lat tightness, and Tracy turned to Miller for the ninth with Garrett Whitlock having a heavy load of late.
Miller allowed a run in the ninth on an infield single, a wild pitch, a walk and a groundout. He loaded the bases after a strikeout got away on a wild pitch, but escaped the jam with a groundout to close it out.
Clinching their postseason spot with a week left in the regular season would allow the Red Sox to breathe and reset some players before the postseason. But they’re not there yet. Saturday awaits.
“It just kind of felt like a playoff game,” Anthony said. “Getting into that mode is huge from an at-bat standpoint and from a big-game standpoint of constantly being the next man up.”

Boston improved to 84-70 with its second consecutive victory and snapped Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak. The Red Sox entered the series opener with a magic number of three to clinch an American League wild-card berth and could secure their postseason spot as early as Saturday.
It was not a comfortable victory.
Red Sox pitchers issued nine walks, including four over the final four innings. The Rays loaded the bases in both the sixth and ninth but went 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and stranded 12 runners. Erik Miller finally ended the ninth-inning adventure by getting Chandler Simpson to ground out with the bases loaded.
Here are three takeaways from Boston's important victory.
Roman Anthony Sets Tone Immediately
Anthony did not wait long to make his presence felt. The Red Sox rookie crushed Ian Seymour's third pitch of the game 438 feet to center field, giving Boston a 1-0 lead before most of the announced crowd of 23,342 had settled into its seats.
It was Anthony's fifth home run of the season and the third leadoff homer of his young career. The Rays answered in the bottom of the first when Junior Caminero drove in Yandy Díaz with a groundout, but Anthony struck again one inning later.
Trevor Story singled and Caleb Durbin followed with another base hit. After Nate Eaton walked to load the bases, Anthony delivered a two-out single to right that scored Story and Durbin. Anthony finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs, accounting for nearly all of Boston's offense on one of the biggest nights of its season.
Jahmai Jones supplied the other run by launching a 414-foot solo homer to left in the third inning. Jones' sixth home run gave Boston a 4-1 advantage that held until the ninth.
Ranger Suárez Bends Without Breaking
Suárez rarely had a clean inning, but the left-hander consistently found his way out of trouble. The Boston starter allowed only three hits and one run while striking out five. He also issued five walks and needed 98 pitches to record 17 outs.
His best defensive moment came in the fourth inning.
Taylor Walls hit a 100-mph line drive directly back at Suárez, who made the catch before throwing to first base to double off Nick Fortes. The play erased a scoring opportunity and helped Suárez navigate another stressful inning. The left-hander improved to 8-4 and lowered his ERA to 3.27.
Wyatt Olds entered with two outs in the sixth and immediately made matters worse by issuing two walks. He recovered to strike out Jake Fraley with the bases loaded, preserving Boston's three-run advantage.
Greg Weissert provided the calmest portion of the night, allowing one hit over two scoreless innings.
Erik Miller Survives Chaotic Ninth Inning
The Red Sox carried a 4-1 lead into the ninth, but Miller turned the final three outs into a full-blown ordeal. The left-hander issued two walks and threw three wild pitches during a 32-pitch inning. Jonathan Aranda drove in one run with a fielder's choice, cutting Boston's lead to 4-2.
Tampa Bay eventually loaded the bases with two outs, bringing Simpson to the plate as the potential winning run. Miller induced a ground ball to third baseman Durbin, who completed the force play at second to end the game. Miller earned his fifth save despite allowing one run, one hit and two walks.
Boston will take the victory, especially at this stage of the season, but the nine walks gave the club another issue to clean up before October. The Red Sox will attempt to clinch their postseason berth Saturday when they continue the three-game series in Tampa Bay. The Rays are scheduled to start right-hander Freddy Peralta, while Boston has yet to announce it's starter.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

ARLINGTON, Texas — When Trevor Story hit his clutch three-run homer to flip a two-run deficit into a one-run lead Thursday against the Rangers, interim manager Chad Tracy didn’t rush to get his two highest-leverage bullpen arms instantly ready. That’s because one of them was unavailable due to a nagging — and previously undisclosed — injury.
With Boston suddenly up, 4-3, Tracy used a pair of rookies (righty Wyatt Olds and lefty Alec Gamboa) to pitch the eighth, then turned things over to righty Garrett Whitlock in the ninth. For at least one night, Whitlock took the job of closer Aroldis Chapman, who has a tight lat muscle.
“He’s just dealing with some lat tightness we’re going to be conservative with,” Tracy said. “It’s getting better, but we’ve got to make sure it gets there. That’s why he wasn’t available tonight.”
Tracy said Chapman — who last pitched Saturday against the Royals — has been dealing with the injury for “a couple of days.” Asked if an injured list stint was possible for the All-Star, Tracy said: “We’re not doing that right now.”
“We’re just going to keep monitoring it and see where he’s at each day,” Tracy said. “Obviously, you know how diligent he is about his prep and getting in and getting treatment, so we’re just monitoring day-to-day.”
Chapman, 38, has had another stellar season in Boston, tallying 34 saves to go along with a 1.95 ERA and 68 strikeouts in 50 ⅔ innings over 52 games. He was one of two key Red Sox players with an injury concern Thursday; first baseman Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit on top of his right hand with a pitch.
Olds, who has a 1.23 ERA and 19 strikeouts in his first 12 MLB appearances since debuting last month, relieved Sonny Gray with one out in the seventh inning and the Sox trailing by two. He got two quick outs before Story’s three-run blast put Boston up 4-3. Olds got Ezequiel Duran to pop out to start the eighth before Gamboa entered for the left-on-left matchup against Corey Seager. Seager singled but Gamboa got Josh Jung to ground into an inning-ending double play five pitches later.
“They were awesome,” Tracy said. “Getting thrust into a big spot, going back out anyways, and then all of the sudden you’re going out with a lead. They did an amazing job.”
Whitlock then recorded his fourth save of the year, needing 12 pitches and getting a similar 6-4-3 double play to end the game.
“He’s great,” Tracy said. “He’s reliable. He’s done it before if Chappy’s down.”

This is why we watch! Trevor Story's season looked dead and buried both three months and three weeks ago. He's battled injury, surgery, rehab, way too many strikeouts, and growing chatter from knuckleheads like me who have repeatedly questioned if he even belongs back in this lineup.
Well tonight, he came to the plate with the Sox down 3-1 in the eighth and on the verge of getting swept. He was facing a tough reliever in Jacob Latz, a Texas team that was 63-1 when leading after seven innings, and the weight of his team going a combined 0-17 with runners in scoring position in the series up to that point.
Then he did this:
As somebody that's been leading the "Trevor Story is cooked " charges, I love this so much! Nothing can humble and amaze quite like baseball, and after months of hard work, grinding behind the scenes, and having to deal with all the noise, Story smashed a 108mph line drive home run not only in the face of Latz and Texas' playoff hopes, but also in the face of all those who have been doubting him for weeks (hand raised).
It's just one game, and the real test doesn't start until the 29th, but boy did this have to feel incredible for Story who hadn't gone deep since May 13th. To do it in that moment, in his home town, and against the backdrop of everything that's happened this year is just so perfectly baseball. It's why we love this game so much, and why people like Story are willing to put in the work behind the scenes for months on end to get the chance to do something amazing like that.
I know some of you might not believe it after what I've written about him in recent weeks, but I truly am very happy for Story! He deserves all the credit tonight!
Oh, and in addition to Story's game changing three-run homer, he followed that up by starting double plays on defense to end both the eighth and ninth:
Baseball really is the best!
Studs
Trevor Story: If I didn't put him here, I'd have to legally resign from Over The Monster.
Wilyer Abreu: He looked a little better tonight with a sharp single in the fourth and a walk that turned into a run on Story's three-run shot.
The bullpen: The comeback wouldn't be complete without the pen holding it down, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable with lat tightness, Wyatt Olds, Alec Gamboa, and Garrett Whitlock combined to go 2.2 scoreless innings.
Duds
Only one dud tonight, and that's me given my recent stance on Story's playing time. The crow is delicious, and I hope it remains on the menu well into October!
One other important note
Just before Story's home run, Willson Contreras was hit in the hand by a pitch and had to leave the game. The good news is x-rays were negative, but given x-rays were also negative after Curtis Mead got hit in July, I'm not going to be celebrating this one until we get further confirmation.
X-rays were negative on Willson Contreras, at least initially, but he remains sore.
Aroldis Chapman was unavailable due to lat tightness and is day-to-day.
Willson Contreras: "Sore. Painful. My hand was numb for like five minutes. That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it’s not a fracture on the top of the bone. I’m just frustrated."

Boston’s Willson Contreras left the game after he was hit by a pitch on his right hand in the eighth inning. Contreras leads the Red Sox with 27 home runs.
Jung hit a solo shot in the first inning to open the scoring. It was his 10th homer of the season.
Texas extended its lead to 3-0 in the third. After two walks and a sacrifice bunt, Jansen singled home Wyatt Langford, and Burger scored on Evan Carter’s sacrifice bunt.
The Red Sox got on the scoreboard in the seventh. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin walked, and Eaton took third on a flyout. A throwing error by second baseman Nicky Lopez on Roman Anthony’s grounder brought in Eaton.

The Boston offense struggled in the first two games of the series. The Red Sox struck out 15 times as the Rangers won 4-2 on Tuesday, and the visitors were held to three hits in a 7-3 loss on Wednesday.

Trevor Story Saves Red Sox From Crushing Sweep With One Swing originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
For seven innings, the Boston Red Sox appeared headed toward a disastrous conclusion to their stay in Texas.
Trevor Story changed everything with one swing.
Story crushed a three-run home run in the eighth inning Thursday night, lifting Boston to a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. The comeback allowed the Red Sox to avoid a three-game sweep and improve to 83-70. Boston entered the seventh inning without a run and trailed 3-0. The Red Sox had managed only three hits through six innings and continued to waste the few scoring opportunities they generated.
Then the game suddenly flipped.
The Red Sox pushed across their first run in the seventh when Nate Eaton scored on a throwing error by Rangers second baseman Nicky Lopez. That cut the deficit to 3-1, but Boston still needed a much bigger response.
Story supplied it one inning later.
Trevor Story Delivers Red Sox's Biggest Swing
Wilyer Abreu opened the eighth with a single before Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch. Isiah Kiner-Falefa entered as a pinch runner, placing two runners aboard with one out.
Story then hammered Jacob Latz's offering 394 feet to left-center field.
The three-run blast turned a 3-1 deficit into a 4-3 advantage. It was Story's fourth home run of the season and accounted for three of Boston's four runs.
Story finished 2-for-4 and produced the Red Sox's only hit in seven at-bats with runners in scoring position. Boston recorded only five hits all night, making Story's timely power even more important.
The late rally rewarded starter Sonny Gray for keeping Boston close after a difficult beginning.
Texas scored once in the first inning on Josh Jung's solo home run before adding two more in the second. Gray settled down from there and held the Rangers scoreless over his final 4 1/3 innings. The veteran right-hander allowed three runs on three hits over 6 1/3 innings. He struck out six and walked three while throwing 102 pitches.
Red Sox Bullpen Protects One-Run Lead
Wyatt Olds recorded the final two outs of the seventh and returned for a scoreless eighth, earning his second victory of the season. Angel Gamboa completed the eighth before Garrett Whitlock handled the ninth. Whitlock issued a walk but did not allow a hit, securing his fourth save.
Boston's defense also turned two double plays, helping its pitching staff hold Texas to four hits.
The victory did not erase the disappointment of losing the first two games of the series. Texas still won the set after taking Monday's opener 4-2 and Tuesday's game 7-3.
It did, however, keep a frustrating trip from becoming a sweep at a critical point in the season.
For most of Thursday night, the Red Sox looked lifeless. Story needed only one pitch to completely rewrite the ending.

This has been a rough stretch for the Red Sox offense, which has effectively turned into a pumpkin after a torrid two months this summer. This week in particular the bats have fallen silent, and for much of Thursday night the Red Sox looked like they were headed toward a discouraging series sweep at the worst possible time.
Things took an especially grim turn when Willson Contreras left the game in the eighth inning after being hit in the hand by a pitch, but while the specter of his absence will loom over the club in the days to come, Trevor Story once again proved that you can never count this Red Sox team out.
The veteran shortstop came through with a go-ahead three-run home run in the top of the eighth inning, flipping the script and giving the Red Sox a badly needed 4-3 win to avoid a sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers.
Story’s shot came with one out against Rangers closer Jacob Latz, completing a three-run comeback and cutting Boston’s magic number to clinch a playoff spot to three with nine games remaining.
“To steal that last one is huge,” Story told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “It’s momentum we can ride out into Tampa.”
Prior to Story’s home run, Thursday was shaping up to be among the club’s worst losses of the season.
A hallmark of the offense’s struggles early in the year was a lot of empty, uncompetitive at-bats, tons of swing and miss and a general inability to make good contact. Even with the Rangers opting for a bullpen game led by Cody Bradford, whose fastball averages just 88.6 mph, the Red Sox couldn’t square anything up.
The Red Sox only managed two hits through the first five innings, both singles in the fourth inning. That put runners at the corners with two outs, but Jarren Duran grounded out to squander the opportunity.
It was a similar story in the sixth, when Wilyer Abreu singled and Adley Rutschman finally did some damage with a ground-rule double into the left-field gap. Had the ball stayed in play, Abreu probably would have scored, but instead the Red Sox had two men in scoring position for Story, who worked a full count and struck out to end the threat.
The offense did nothing to pick up Sonny Gray, who wasn’t perfect but did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
The veteran right-hander allowed a solo home run to Josh Jung with two outs in the first, and in the second he walked the first two batters of the inning, both of whom came around to score on an RBI bloop single by Danny Jansen and a run-scoring squeeze bunt by Evan Carter.
Gray settled down afterward and retired 14 of the last 16 batters he faced from the second inning into the seventh. He was charged with three runs over 6 1/3 innings and limited the Rangers to three hits and three walks with six strikeouts.
“I thought he was awesome,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said. “The only blemish was the two walks, we kind of walked ourselves into the part of their lineup where they can play baseball a little bit with bunts and they drop a flare into center and there’s a safety squeeze, outside of that, that was a really, really good effort.”
Even when the Red Sox finally scored in the top of the seventh, they did so without recording a hit. Nate Eaton and Caleb Durbin led off with consecutive walks and Eaton advanced to third after Nick Sogard hit a rocket of a fly out to the center field wall. But with one out and a chance to fight back into the game, Roman Anthony grounded into a run-scoring fielder’s choice to make it 3-1. He advanced to second after the Rangers threw away the double-play attempt, but Mickey Gasper grounded out to end the inning.
Then came the eighth.
Once again the Red Sox got two men on base right away, with Abreu drawing a leadoff walk before Contreras was hit in the right hand by a pitch. He immediately left the game with the trainer and was replaced at first by Isiah Kiner-Falefa, but while the Red Sox worried about their slugger, the Rangers pulled Jakob Junis for their closer Latz, who has been among the most dominant closers in the American League this year.
Latz drew a pop out from Rutschman, but then Story stepped up to the plate and everything changed.
“You see one of our guys keeled over holding his hand and you’re down in the dumps seeing that and moments later the whole dugout erupts,” Tracy said. “We haven’t been doing much offensively for a few days and to get a swing right there and feel like you steal a game, it was enormous. Big emotion swing.”
With the lead in hand, Wyatt Olds and Alec Gamboa pitched a scoreless eighth, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable, Garrett Whitlock came on for the ninth and locked down the save for the win. Story and Sogard turned inning-ending double plays in both the eighth and the ninth to ensure the Rangers couldn’t mount one last comeback.
“Good teams find a way to win and we’ve been doing that in the second half and that’s kind of who you become,” Story said. “And you feel that momentum, you feel that vibe around the game and we never give up.”
X-rays negative, Chapman day-to-day
The Red Sox got some good news postgame when X-rays on Contreras’ hand came back negative.
“He’s got a bruise on the hand and some swelling,” Tracy said. “So we’ll just take it day to day and see how he is.”
Tracy also confirmed that Chapman has been dealing with some lat tightness for the past few days and they are taking a conservative approach.
“It’s getting better but have to make sure it gets there, that’s why he wasn’t available tonight,” Tracy said, adding that an IL stint isn’t being considered for Chapman right now.

Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
